ports.name: code
ports.description: 3-bit binary code of the highest-priority set bit (bit 7 highest, bit 0 lowest)

ports.name: valid
ports.description: Asserted high when at least one input bit is set; low when in == 8'b0

rtl_spec.behavior:
Purely combinational priority encoder. The output 'code' reflects the index (0-7) of the most-significant '1' in 'in'. Bit 7 has highest priority, bit 0 lowest. When 'in' == 8'b0000_0000, 'code' == 3'b000 and 'valid' == 1'b0. For any non-zero 'in', 'valid' == 1'b1 and 'code' is the position of the highest set bit. Truth table (selected rows):
  in=8'b1xxxxxxx -> code=3'd7, valid=1
  in=8'b01xxxxxx -> code=3'd6, valid=1
  in=8'b001xxxxx -> code=3'd5, valid=1
  in=8'b0001xxxx -> code=3'd4, valid=1
  in=8'b00001xxx -> code=3'd3, valid=1
  in=8'b000001xx -> code=3'd2, valid=1
  in=8'b0000001x -> code=3'd1, valid=1
  in=8'b00000001 -> code=3'd0, valid=1
  in=8'b00000000 -> code=3'd0, valid=0
constraints: Combinational logic only (no clocks, no registers)
Outputs must update immediately when inputs change

rtl_code:
module priority_encoder_8to3 (
    input  wire [7:0] in,
    output reg  [2:0] code,
    output reg        valid
);

    always @(*) begin
        code  = 3'd0;
        valid = 1'b0;

        casez (in)
            8'b1???????: begin code = 3'd7; valid = 1'b1; end
            8'b01??????: begin code = 3'd6; valid = 1'b1; end
            8'b001?????: begin code = 3'd5; valid = 1'b1; end
            8'b0001????: begin code = 3'd4; valid = 1'b1; end
            8'b00001???: begin code = 3'd3; valid = 1'b1; end
            8'b000001??: begin code = 3'd2; valid = 1'b1; end
            8'b0000001?: begin code = 3'd1; valid = 1'b1; end
            8'b00000001: begin code = 3'd0; valid = 1'b1; end
            default:     begin code = 3'd0; valid = 1'b0; end
        endcase
    end

endmodule
explanation: This module implements an 8-to-3 priority encoder that identifies the most significant set bit in the 8-bit input vector and outputs its binary index (0-7) along with a valid flag indicating any bit was set. The combinational logic uses a `casez` statement with descending priority patterns to efficiently infer a priority chain, ensuring the highest-order '1' takes precedence over lower bits. Default assignments at the start of the `always` block guarantee defined outputs for the all-zero input case, preventing latches and ensuring the valid flag correctly deasserts when no inputs are active.
